summary: This is a hill, and for its first thirty years the record is the city trying to get streets onto it. The Board kept re-setting the official grades on Saturn, Temple and Lower Terrace, licensed contractors to set off blasts on Upper Terrace, and where a roadway would not go it ordered a stairway instead — one from the low level of Ord Street up to Market in 1931. The flat ground at the bottom held the horses: 184 of them at the United Milk Company's stable on Sixteenth Street in 1915, sixty more behind 125-135 Landers Street the year before. Until about 1930 the Board also voted on every fuel-oil tank and boiler, so the record names the shops one at a time — the Original Fairville Creamery heating water for its dairy at 444 Castro Street, Hugo's Pastry Shop at 524, the Eureka Valley Bakery over on Eighteenth. Two schools went up and their land was bought a parcel at a time, Mission High on Dolores Street and Everett on Sanchez, where the Board was still paying out of the school tax for one lot after another in 1923. The Twin Peaks Tunnel was driven under the ridge, and by 1914 the City Attorney was advising on how to avoid damage suits from the ground above it; a storm in February 1969 washed out fifty-two feet of sewer under Douglass Street. When the Market Street Railway asked in 1938 to stop running its cars up Castro Street, the Board said no. The Castro that people come to see arrives late and in ordinary paperwork — a street closed for a fair in 1975, Supervisor Milk asking in 1978 for a fence behind the streetcar stop at Market and Castro, the street closed for an AIDS vigil in 1983, the rainbow flag at Harvey Milk Plaza made a landmark in 2024 — and running under all of it, from that same year 1975, a steady line of condominium maps.
